title: Invitations and تعارف — the courtesy you're meant to refuse
goal: Invite, accept, and decline — and understand an Iranian custom that, if misread, can make you look greedy or rude.
bekal: invite someone and respond to an invitation the right way
recognize تعارف and know how many times to say no

dialogs.title: گفتگو — دعوت به شام
dialogs.intro: Maryam invites Budi to dinner at her family's home. Budi doesn't know yet that this conversation has rules of its own.

notes: ⚠️ **The custom تعارف is a ritual of layered offering and refusing, and it governs nearly every social situation in Iran.** It works like this: the person offering must offer more than they mean, and the person offered must refuse several times before accepting. The mistake isn't accepting — it's accepting **too quickly**.

**A rule of thumb that almost always works: refuse twice, accept the third time.** If an offer is repeated three times in earnest, it's real. If it's made once and never repeated, it was just politeness.

⚠️ **And the costly exception: a shopkeeper's or driver's تعارف is never real.** The seller's قابل نداره ("no need to pay") — which you met in unit 7 — is pure courtesy. The answer isn't to say thanks and leave, but to ask the price again. This is the only kind of تعارف that can get you into real trouble.
**The phrase با کمالِ میل = "with pleasure"**, literally "with the perfection of desire". The most polite way to accept an invitation, and worth memorizing whole.

⚠️ **"Don't bring anything" (چیزی نیاورید) is تعارف, and you must still bring something.** The usual choices: شیرینی (a box of pastries), گل (flowers), or میوه (fruit). Showing up empty-handed at an Iranian home is one of the few things that truly looks bad.
**Spoken forms:** جمعه شب بیاین خونهٔ ما (*jom'e shab biyâyn khune-ye mâ*), مزاحمتون می‌شم (*mozâhemetun misham*), این چه حرفیه! (*in che harfiye!*), با کمالِ میل (unchanged).

grammars.title: Inviting, accepting, declining
after: **Turning down a real invitation takes a reason and regret**, not just "no". A safe pattern: **regret + reason + hope for next time** — متأسفانه نمی‌توانم، کار دارم. ایشالله دفعهٔ بعد.
**A plain "no" (نه ساده) is almost never used on its own** to turn down an invitation. It sounds cold, even rude. Even a firm refusal is wrapped in شرمنده or متأسفانه.

grammars.title: Reading تعارف: real or not?
after: **Signs of a real offer:** it's repeated more than twice, comes with details (time, date, address), or with body language — the person actually stands up, grabs their keys, pulls out their phone.
**Signs of pure courtesy:** it's said once, with no details, and the conversation moves straight on to something else.
And the most helpful tip: **when in doubt, refuse once more.** Refusing one time too many hurts no one; accepting one time too soon can make things awkward.

grammars.title: Words and phrases that smooth everything over
after: Six of these ten phrases are Arabic loans used across much of the Muslim world. Saying them is easy — what you need to learn is when Iranians use them, and that comes with practice.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Arriving on time for an Iranian dinner invitation is actually too early.** Arriving fifteen to thirty minutes after the stated time is normal, and the host expects it. If you show up at eight sharp, there's a real chance your host is still in the shower. Formal appointments are the opposite: they run exactly on time.

blocks.title: What to bring, and what not to
items: **Always right:** a box of شیرینی from a pastry shop (not homemade unless you've been asked), a bouquet of flowers, or a basket of fruit.
**What not to bring:** alcohol (it isn't sold and isn't wanted), and don't bring a main dish unless asked — it can read as if you doubt the host's cooking.
**If there are children in the home**, bringing a small something for them is always warmly received.

blocks.title: For Muslim travelers: two things you don't need to worry about
items: **Halal food is the default in Iran.** No restaurant serves pork, and alcohol isn't served in public or in most homes. The worries that come with travel to many other countries don't apply here.

**Prayer times are easy to keep.** Mosques are everywhere, many offices and shopping malls have a نمازخانه (prayer room), and no one will think it odd if you excuse yourself for a moment. The sentence: ببخشید، برایِ نماز می‌روم ("excuse me, I'm going to pray").
Thank you for the invitation.
With pleasure.
Unfortunately I can't.
I'm full, thank you.
God willing, next time.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right تعارف phrase.
items: Replying to praise of your Persian: ____ دارید.
Thanking a host who cooked: دستتان ____ نکند.
To someone who has just finished working: ____ نباشید.
Turning down a fourth cup of tea: ____ است، ممنون.
Accepting an invitation politely: با کمالِ ____.

exercises.prompt: Real or just تعارف? Write واقعی or تعارف.
items: A shopkeeper says قابل نداره: ____
A host says چیزی نیاورید: ____
A host repeats the invitation three times, with a date and time: ____
A landlord says خانهٔ خودتان است: ____
A friend stands up, grabs the car keys, and says می‌رسانمتان: ____

wave: Practice four invitation sentences until they come out without thinking: مزاحمتان می‌شوم / این چه حرفی است / با کمالِ میل / لازم نیست. Two minutes a day for a week.
